title: Paul Blart, Eight-year-old Cat At Yellowstone Valley Animal Shelter, Ready For Adoption At No Cost - Montana Talks
content: I will admit that when I was much younger, I thought all cats basically had the same personality. We had farm cats when I was a kid, but they weren't very pet-like, and I don't remember ever having an indoor cat growing up. Of course, cats have unique personalities just as much as dogs, and our featured adoptable Wet Nose Wednesday Pet this week is a perfect example. His name is Paul Blart, and he's a real character. Read More: Why Feeding Bears Can Be Dangerous In Montana Arriving at Yellowstone Valley Animal Shelter as a stray, this curious kitty is a bit on the chunky side, much like his movie mall cop namesake. Paul Blart didn't seem to mind his travel carrier one bit, and after a minute or two, he popped out to explore. We asked Izzy Zalenski, Community Engagement Coordinator at YVAS, if those old reports of people adopting and doing nefarious things with black cats around Halloween are still a thing, or more like an urban legend. Thankfully, it's pretty much not an issue, said Zalenski, with little to no current data or reports to reflect otherwise. Someone has sponsored the adoption fee for Paul Blart, which means you can take him into your loving home for FREE. Thank you, Advanced Employment, for being a part of Wet Nose Wednesday. title: Lansing’s Massive New Total Wine & More Is Finally Here - 1240 The Ticket
content: And don't worry, they can help you out with that too... They, being Total Wine & More! Lansing has been waiting for Total Wine & More to open in Frandor since we first saw Frandor teasing us with the announcement on social media back in May this year. Now, the wait is finally over, as Total Wine & More opened at the end of September. If you're looking for a particular 21-and-older beverage to quench your thirst, the likelihood that Total Wine & More has it is pretty high. This gigantic beverage store is home to just about any beer, wine, spirits or mixer that you can think of. They have products from all over the world. And keep in mind, it's located in the former Joann Fabrics, which closed in May 2025. Remember how big that store was? Imagine that, but instead of bunches of yarn and paint supplies, it's filled with alcohol. There's something for every taste and budget. If you want something that's made in Michigan, there's a huge selection of Mitten-made products. If you want something that comes in a really cool bottle, there are plenty of options. From spirits that were made with spooky movies in mind... To bottles of liquor that are as much as a mortgage payment... it's almost a little overwhelming how much Total Wine & More has to offer. Not to mention, if you're ever curious about what a beverage tastes like before spending money on a big bottle, there are tastings on Thursdays, Fridays, and Saturdays. You must be 21 or older with a valid ID. And of course, always remember to drink responsibly. Especially because you still need to brave the Frandor parking lot to get home.

Global wafer foundry leader Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US) is evaluating a potential investment in Texas to expand its chip production in the United States. Zhitong Finance APP learned that Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US), the global leader in wafer foundry services, is evaluating a potential investment in Texas to expand its chip production in the United States. According to foreign media citing sources familiar with the matter, this potential investment would be an additional initiative beyond the $265 billion that Taiwan Semiconductor has already committed to its Arizona operations; the relevant plans have not yet been finalized. According to Taiwanese media citing sources from the semiconductor equipment supply chain, Taiwan Semiconductor is evaluating the construction of a second large-scale manufacturing campus in the United States, with plans to build up to six advanced wafer fabs. Potential locations include the Dallas and North Texas areas, and the investment could exceed that of the Arizona facility. Choosing Texas was no accident. Dallas and North Texas are known as the "Silicon Prairie," having developed a mature industrial cluster for semiconductor manufacturing, silicon wafer supply chains, optical communications, and defense-related industries. Major companies such as Texas Instruments, Samsung, Coherent, and Tesla have all established factories there. Wells Fargo & Co. analyst Joe Quatrochi noted that the region already hosts several wafer fabs, making it a logical location for Taiwan Semiconductor to establish its second campus. Moreover, Texas's advantages in land, energy, and talent are highly attractive to energy-intensive advanced wafer fabs. From a strategic perspective, the expansion of 2-nanometer capacity is a key highlight. Taiwan Semiconductor's 2-nanometer process is expected to begin contributing initial revenue in the second quarter of 2026, with major customers including Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, and Qualcomm. As these key clients increase their order volumes by 10% to 20%, Taiwan Semiconductor is accelerating its capacity expansion; monthly 2-nanometer production could reach 120,000 wafers by year-end, surpassing the previous market estimate of 90,000 to 100,000 wafers. The production capacity originally slated for 2027 may now be achieved ahead of schedule. Quatrochi stated that if this expansion materializes, it should be viewed as a potential positive catalyst for semiconductor equipment companies. Customer demand and policy pressure together serve as the dual drivers behind Taiwan Semiconductor's increased investment in U.S. manufacturing. In the first half of 2026, U.S. customers will account for approximately 75.64% of Taiwan Semiconductor's revenue. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has continued to press chipmakers to relocate production capacity to the United States, threatening to impose tariffs as high as 200% on companies that fail to establish factories in the U.S., thereby further encouraging Taiwan Semiconductor to expand its presence in the country. In terms of market impact, if Taiwan Semiconductor launches its second campus in Texas, it will link Arizona's wafer manufacturing with Texas's advanced ecosystem, establishing a two‑major‑manufacturing‑base structure in the United States and benefiting the semiconductor equipment supply chain. However, the specific plans for the six fabs, the investment amounts, and the process nodes have not yet been officially confirmed. Supply-chain players believe that site‑selection assessments are nearing completion, but Taiwan Semiconductor's Director has not yet made a final decision. In July, Taiwan Semiconductor announced an additional $100 billion investment in Arizona, bringing its total planned investment in the state to $265 billion. This expansion is expected to add four semiconductor manufacturing and packaging facilities, increasing its total number of U.S. facilities to 12. Taiwan Semiconductor's first U.S. chip fab in Phoenix began mass production of 4-nanometer chips at the end of 2024. Its second fab is expected to start producing more advanced 3-nanometer chips in the second half of next year. title: TSM Stock Spikes Overnight: Q1 Print Tops Estimates On Strong Demand For AI Chips, Advanced Processors - Stocktwits
content: U.S.-listed shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM) rose over 1% in overnight trading early Thursday after the chipmaker beat first-quarter (Q1) estimates on both revenue and profit as strong demand for 3nm chips and high-performance computing (HPC) continued to drive growth. TSM stock fell over 1% to $375.1 on Wednesday, but climbed marginally in extended trading. TSM reported net income of NT$572.48 billion ($18.14 billion) in Q1, up 58% from the previous year and above Fiscal AI estimates of NT$553.4 billion, while diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at NT$22.08, exceeding estimates of NT$20.96. The company also reported revenue of NT$1.134 trillion, rising 35% from a year ago and ahead of estimates of NT$1.117 trillion. Advanced process tech remained the backbone of TSM’s revenue growth during the quarter. 3-nanometer chips accounted for 25% of wafer revenue, while 5-nanometer chips contributed 36% and 7-nanometer chips represented 13%, with 7nm and more advanced technologies making up 74% of total wafer revenue. In U.S. dollar terms, quarterly revenue hit $35.9 billion, rising 41% from a year ago and 6.4% from the previous quarter. Meanwhile, gross margin for the quarter came in at 66%, operating margin reached 58%, and net profit margin stood at 51%. HPC continued to dominate the company’s revenue mix. The segment accounted for 61% of total revenue, underscoring its role as TSM’s largest growth engine, as AI-related workloads drive strong semiconductor demand. Smartphones contributed 26% of revenue, while IoT accounted for 6% and automotive for 4%. Revenue from high-performance computing increased 20% from the previous quarter, while smartphone revenue declined 11% from the prior quarter. title: The Real Reasons Sierra Vista Roads Frustrate People - allhitskzmk.com
content: I was scrolling through a local Facebook group recently and saw a discussion about the major roads in Sierra Vista. Residents debated whether the city's street layout makes driving more difficult and whether it affects safety. While opinions varied, a few common concerns appeared throughout the conversation, including sun glare, the city's grid design, and traffic accidents. One of the most common complaints about driving in Sierra Vista has less to do with the roads themselves and more to do with the sun. Many major roads run east-west, meaning drivers can find themselves looking directly into the rising or setting sun. Unlike potholes or congestion, sun glare is not a problem that can be quickly fixed. Arizona receives more sunshine a year than any other state, and drivers often encounter glare during the busiest travel times of the day. For residents who regularly travel east in the morning or west in the evening, frustration with certain roads is understandable. READ: Cochise County's Snowbird Season: Impact On Local Economy The majority of roads in Sierra Vista follow a grid layout. This common street design uses roads that generally run north-south and east-west, creating a network of blocks that makes navigation relatively straightforward. For newcomers, it's often easy to find alternate routes and understand how different parts of the city connect. While most of the roads follow this pattern, the Sierra Vista's road network is not entirely uniform. According ot the city's website, some neighborhoods and intersections were developed before modern planning standards were adopted, resulting in a mix of street designs. That combination of older roads and newer development may help explain why residents have such different opinions about the city's streets. READ: How Hot Do Parked Cars Get In Arizona's Summer Heat I am not going to lie, I have seen my fair share of bad drivers in Sierra Vista. Whether it's speeding, running red lights, failing to use turn signals, or simply not paying attention, most local drivers have a story about a close call on the road. However, the statistics suggest the city may not be as dangerous to drive in as some residents believe. According to US Crime Data, Sierra Vista experiences 8.2 traffic deaths per 100,000 residents annually. The national average is 12.3 deaths per 100,000 residents, putting Sierra Vista well below the national rate. While no fatal crash is acceptable, the numbers suggest that despite residents' frustrations with local drivers, Sierra Vista's roads are generally safer than many communities across the country. So, are Sierra Vista's roads badly designed? The answer depends on who you ask. Some frustrations, such as blinding sunlight during rush hour and packed intersections, are very real. Others come down to personal preferences or individual driving experiences. Whether you love the city's road layout or dislike it, nearly everyone in Sierra Vista has something to say about the roads they travel on every day. title: Bottlenecking the Future: TSMC Prices Out the Competition - MarketBeat
content:
The market often debates the durability of the semiconductor hardware cycle. Market skeptics point to macroeconomic slowing, cyclical financing, and inventory gluts as reasons to discount chipmakers. Yet, the leading indicator for global computing infrastructure is telling a different story entirely. If we examine the capital and capacity flows at the foundational layer of chip fabrication, a clearer picture of a sustained, multi-year demand signal is emerging. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company NYSE: TSM is actively accelerating its 2-nanometer production timeline, effectively cornering the global advanced computing supply chain. Instead of pulling back on capital expenditures amid economic uncertainty, the leading chip fabricator is pressing the accelerator, backed by direct commitments from the world's largest technology firms. This divergence between market anxiety and hard production data offers a compelling opportunity for investors evaluating the semiconductor space. When a foundry of this scale pulls forward capacity, it does so based on signed agreements, not speculative forecasts. TSMC's shift to accelerate its 2-nanometer production signals that the top tier of the semiconductor market operates independently of standard consumer electronics cycles. To understand the foundational strength of the current semiconductor cycle, we look directly at TSMC's plans for its 2-nanometer node. Recently, production targets for this process were revised upward by roughly 20%, aiming for around 120,000 wafers per month by the end of 2026. This target shift from an earlier baseline of 100,000 wafers highlights a critical business reality for the fabrication industry. Semiconductor capital expenditure at this level is demand-driven. Foundries expand capacity because guaranteed, locked-in client orders demand that physical space. The fundamental advantage here centers on pricing power. Early estimates suggest that an advanced 2-nanometer wafer will command a premium price approaching $30,000. Compared with the 3-nanometer node, which prices around $20,000, this represents a 50% premium. For investors, this pricing dynamic is central to the semiconductor investment thesis. Moving clients to the latest node lets TSMC organically expand margins even if total global wafer volume growth stabilizes. Foundries operating at the bleeding edge do not compete on price; they compete on physics. By accelerating its 2nm timeline, TSMC widens its lead over competitors, making it the default choice for companies designing next-generation chips. A fabrication business's true strength depends entirely on the quality and necessity of its clients. Currently, early tape-outs for the 2-nanometer node are registering at roughly four times the volume seen during the equivalent developmental stage of the previous iteration. For context, a tape-out is the final stage of the chip design process before physical manufacturing begins. This metric is a leading indicator of future revenue visibility. Captive clients like Apple NASDAQ: AAPL, NVIDIA NASDAQ: NVDA, and Advanced Micro Devices NASDAQ: AMD are locked in an architectural arms race. Because training advanced models and operating high-performance computing centers require maximizing silicon efficiency, these developers cannot afford to wait for alternative foundries to catch up. They are often willing to pay a premium to secure early capacity. This dynamic positions TSMC as a toll road for next-generation hardware. When a single company controls most of the world's supply of its most critical technological component, concerns about a cyclical hardware slowdown lose their weight. The broader semiconductor market might experience inventory cycles in the automotive sector or standard consumer electronics, but the top-tier computing fabrication market operates on an isolated demand curve. Institutional positioning further confirms the thesis. A review of recent options chain data shows implied volatility lingering in the low 30% range, paired with a volume put-call ratio near 0.80. This lack of heavy downside hedging indicates that institutional capital remains firmly anchored to the bullish narrative. Short interest in TSMC stock is virtually nonexistent, representing less than 1% of the total float. Corporate leadership is signaling a similar confidence. Recent regulatory filings indicate executive open-market purchases, including direct stock acquisitions by the CEO. When an insider allocates personal capital to a stock that is already significantly up, it typically signals internal conviction about forward-looking capacity and revenue pipelines. Institutional investors seem to share this sentiment, with entities like Silicon Valley Capital Partners recently initiating multi-million-dollar positions to capture the upcoming margin expansion. From a valuation standpoint, TSMC's forward price-to-earnings ratio in the upper 20s presents an interesting relative discount. While fabless client partners like Advanced Micro Devices trade at forward multiples near 80x, the company building the physical architecture trades at a far more conservative valuation, despite net margins routinely hovering around 50%. No company operates without friction, and one variable for investors to monitor is the cost of TSMC's geographic diversification. Supply chain reports indicate active evaluations for expanding mega-campus footprints, including potential secondary sites in the United States. Building fabrication facilities outside Taiwan's established ecosystem raises operating costs, exacerbates specialized labor shortages, and complicates logistics. These factors will likely put pressure on gross margins during the initial build-out phase. However, investors who evaluate TSMC on short-term margin compression alone are overlooking the broader strategic pivot. Spreading production across regions reduces the company's dependence on a single geography, addressing one of the main reasons cautious institutional investors have long discounted the stock. The unparalleled pricing leverage of the 2-nanometer node will help offset the capital expenditure burden of international expansion. TSMC's recent revenue acceleration, highlighted by a year-over-year jump exceeding 50% in late summer 2026, demonstrates how easily premium pricing can absorb higher operating costs. Management's upward revision to full-year revenue growth guidance cements this reality. By securing dominant pricing power and locking in multi-year capacity commitments from the world's best-funded technology developers, TSMC has laid the foundation for lasting leadership. For investors watching the hardware cycle, the toll road for the digital economy is getting wider, and the barriers to entry have never been higher. title: Why Some Grand Rapids Residents Absolutely Hate ArtPrize - 97.9 WGRD
content: ArtPrize has been a fixture in Grand Rapids since it launched in 2009. Many residents love it, while others absolutely hate it. Find out why from a recent online debate. ArtPrize was founded by entrepreneur Rick DeVos as a radically open, independently organized international public art competition. The idea was to shake things up by moving away from traditional, highly curated gallery settings. There were no selection committees, and artists from around the world could enter. Even better, the public got to vote for their favorite works, with the winners taking home some seriously big cash prizes. Since launching in 2009, ArtPrize has evolved through several different formats, including a 2019 Project 1 and a pandemic-related pause in 2020. Read More: New Grand Rapids ArtPrize Mural Transforms Tagged Wall As impressive as some of the artwork at ArtPrize can be, not everyone in Grand Rapids is a fan of the event. Recently, someone on the Grand Rapids subreddit asked if there were any ArtPrize haters out there, and plenty of people jumped in to share their thoughts. Depending on the weather, ArtPrize can draw some pretty big crowds to downtown Grand Rapids, especially on the weekends. Several commenters said that ArtPrize has moved away from its local roots, with some commenters saying the event now features more artists from outside the area. AI was another issue that frustrated some commenters during ArtPrize 2026. A few people in the subreddit thread even described ArtPrize as more of a tourist trap than anything else. Several downtown workers said ArtPrize makes their daily routine a little more difficult, from heavier traffic and fewer parking spots to packed restaurants during their lunch breaks. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global semiconductor foundry market was worth $175.1 billion in 2025 and is projected to witness a 3.4% CAGR between 2026 and 2034. The growth of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, 5G and the Internet of Things (IoT) is creating demand for more advanced semiconductor technologies, prompting foundries to heavily invest in research and development and develop new process nodes. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company TSM, or TSMC, and United Microelectronics Corporation UMC are among the established names competing in this market. TSMC continues to hold a commanding position, accounting for nearly 73% of the global market in the second quarter of 2026, based on insights from Counterpoint Research. The company's revenues are heavily tied to customers serving high-performance computing (HPC), smartphones, IoT, automotive and digital consumer electronics. Meanwhile, United Microelectronics maintained a 4% market share for the fourth consecutive quarter. The company derives most of its operating revenues from manufacturing chips for communication devices, consumer electronics, PCs and other computers. Both stocks have trailed the broader sector over the past three months, although TSMC has fared better than UMC. Here's a closer look at where the two companies stand today. TSMC benefits from sustained AI and high-performance computing demand, with its leading-edge technologies driving growth. Management expects strong demand for leading-edge technologies and continued cost improvements to help offset the near-term margin impact from the steep 2-nanometer (N2) ramp-up. The AI megatrend continues to drive demand for more computing and leading-edge silicon. TSMC said its customers and their customers, mainly cloud service providers, continue to provide a strong signal and positive outlook. The rise of Agentic AI is boosting the role of CPUs in AI data centers, adding to silicon demand beyond AI accelerators and providing another growth opportunity for the company. At the same time, TSMC's additional $100 billion investment in Arizona, backed by its leading U.S. customers and federal, state and local governments, will support several more fabs for N2 and below technologies and advanced packaging. The company is also adding three 3-nanometer (N3) fabs in Taiwan, Arizona and Japan while converting 5-nanometer tools to support N3 capacity in Taiwan. Customer interest and engagement in TSMC's A14 technology remain strong across smartphone and HPC AI applications, with tape-out activity ongoing and ahead of schedule. Pre-production will start in 2027, and volume production is scheduled for 2028. A14 could become a more significant and longer-lasting node family than N2, according to management, extending TSMC's technology roadmap. TSMC is also working with ASML Holding N.V. on the semiconductor industry's transition to larger-format Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography photomasks. The move is expected to further increase fab productivity, lower chipmaking costs and remove stitching constraints, supporting the development of smaller, faster and more energy-efficient chips. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for TSMC's 2026 EPS currently stands at $16.56, implying a 55.5% jump over 2025. The estimate has seen an upward revision over the past 60 days. UMC's second-quarter 2026 revenues grew 12.6% sequentially to reach TWD 68.7 billion. Revenues from its 22/28nm business continue to set records, with 22nm revenues reaching 17.5% of second-quarter sales. For the third quarter, the company expects stable demand across the computer, communications and consumer segments, with shipments projected to increase at a high-single-digit rate, driven by strong demand for power management ICs, sensors and microcontrollers. Its 8-inch portfolio is also seeing a strong rebound, with utilization expected to improve significantly. United Microelectronics' AI-related business is driven by the specialty semiconductor solution, supporting a broad range of applications, including power management, connectivity, FPGA, advanced packaging and silicon photonics. This business is expected to become an important contributor to growth in 2026, with current annual revenues projected to be roughly $300 million. Over the next three years, UMC expects its AI exposure to exceed $1 billion. In late July, the company's board of directors approved a phased expansion plan that includes expanding cleanroom capacity in Singapore and starting construction of a new fab building shell at its flagship Tainan campus in Taiwan. The dual-track plan is aimed at meeting near-term customer demand while creating the footprint needed to support future high-growth AI and edge-computing applications. As a result, the 2026 capital expenditure budget was increased to $2 billion from $1.5 billion. The company also announced the first mass-production wafer delivery of photonic ICs from its Singapore fab, combining SILITH's silicon photonics innovation. The milestone demonstrates the company's high-volume silicon photonics manufacturing capabilities on 12-inch wafers. The consensus mark for United Microelectronics' 2026 EPS implies year-over-year growth of 132.1% to $1.23, with the estimate moving higher over the past 60 days. Based on forward 12-month Price/Earnings (P/E), TSM trades at 22.51X, roughly a 7% discount to its historical median of 24.21X. UMC, meanwhile, is trading at 21.45X P/E, nearly a 23.3% premium to its median of 17.40X. TSMC is well positioned to benefit from sustained AI demand and the growing need for leading-edge computing power. The company is stepping up capacity investments while advancing its A14 technology. Meanwhile, UMC's growth is being supported by record 22nm revenues, strong demand for power management ICs and a rebound in 8-inch utilization. Its AI-related business is also poised to play a larger role in growth. Both foundry players are expected to see strong earnings momentum in 2026. Valuation also favors TSMC, which trades below its historical median P/E, while UMC trades at a premium. Supported by its recent price performance, TSM is the stronger investment choice right now. content: This weekend, we worked with a couple of neighbors to install a new water tank on our well and get the pipes ready for winter. First, we had to move a large prickly pear cactus that had taken root nearby. Our neighbor, who knows his way around a garden, took care of removing and dividing it for replanting. Since prickly pears can be moved pretty easily, and this one was huge, I started looking up recipes for both the paddles (nopales) and the fruit (tunas). Now I have a few ideas. One of Arizona’s most prolific cacti might already be growing in your backyard, too. If you’ve ever had prickly pear candy, jelly, syrup, or even a margarita, you know this desert plant has a unique flavor. What surprises many people is that you can eat both the pads and the fruit. The flat green pads are called nopales. You have to carefully remove the spines, either by scraping or carefully burning them off in an open flame. Then you can use them in all kinds of dishes. I’ve even seen them for sale in some of our specialty grocery stores. People chop nopales for tacos, grill them as a side, or add them to scrambled eggs and breakfast burritos. They’re mild and a bit tangy, with a texture like green beans or asparagus. For generations, nopales have been a staple in Southwestern and Mexican cooking, turning an ordinary desert cactus into something delicious. READ: What Happened When Canadians Asked: "What Foods Are Uniquely AZ?" Prickly pear fruit—called tunas—ripens in late summer and is bright red or purple. The flavor is sweet and often described as a mix of watermelon, berries, and a little bubblegum. You can turn the fruit into juice, jelly, syrup, or candy. Around here, prickly pear syrup goes into lemonade, barbecue sauce, glazes, desserts, and cocktails. If you're planning to harvest prickly pear, be extra careful. Thick gloves and tongs are a must because the cactus is covered in tiny spines called glochids, and once they're embedded in your skin, they're really difficult to remove. The effort of harvesting prickly pear is worth it, though. From breakfast tacos with nopales to homemade prickly pear jelly , this is a true Arizona flavor that’s hard to find anywhere else. title: The Surprising Climate Along the San Pedro - allhitskzmk.com
content: This morning I decided to stop by the San Pedro River to take some pictures. When I left the radio station, the temperature was nice; there were some clouds in the sky, but no sign of rain. However, as soon as I reached the San Pedro House, the weather did a complete 180. The difference was so noticeable that it felt like I had traveled to a completely different part of the state. Experiences like this are common along the San Pedro River, thanks to the area's unique microclimate. READ: SABO's Hummingbird Banding Program Near Sierra Vista Explained A microclimate is a small region where the weather and climate differ significantly from the surrounding area. They are created by changes in topography, the presence of water, and the density of plant cover. Microclimates can create noticeably different conditions within a short distance, resulting in cooler temperatures, higher humidity, or reduced wind. The drive from the radio station to the San Pedro River is less than 8 miles, or around 15 minutes. The temperature was 80 degrees when I left Sierra Vista, and only 59 degrees when I got to the river. This 20-degree drop in temperature was the result of the San Pedro River's microclimate. RELATED: How Beavers Support Ecosystems Along The San Pedro River The San Pedro River's microclimate does more than change the weather. It also supports one of the most diverse ecosystems in the Southwest. The cooler temperatures and higher moisture levels allow cottonwood and willow forests to thrive, creating habitat for hundreds of species of birds, mammals, reptiles, and insects. This ribbon of water through the desert provides a vital refuge for wildlife and makes the river a popular destination for hikers, birdwatchers, and nature photographers. Without its unique microclimate, the San Pedro would look and feel very different from the lush, wildlife-filled corridor visitors experience today. READ MORE: Hereford Bridge, One Of Southern Arizona's Last One-lane Crossings My quick trip to the San Pedro this morning serves as a reminder that the river's microclimate can transform an ordinary day outdoors into an unexpected adventure. Thanks to its unique microclimate, the river corridor remains a cool, green oasis, shaping not only the local weather but also the wildlife and landscapes that make the San Pedro so special. title: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) Stock Climbs as Major Clients Boost 2nm Chip Orders by 20% - Blockonomi
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. is accelerating the rollout of its cutting-edge semiconductor technology. Despite the positive developments, TSM stock dipped 0.12%, though underlying demand fundamentals remain robust. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited, TSM Reports from Taiwanese tech publication EDN indicate that TSMC’s 2-nanometer production capacity could climb to approximately 120,000 wafers monthly by year-end 2026. This figure significantly exceeds previous industry forecasts ranging between 90,000 and 100,000 wafers. The expansion stems from a straightforward factor: customer demand has outpaced initial projections. According to EDN’s reporting, major clients including Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, and MediaTek have expanded their 2nm semiconductor orders. These order increases span between 10% and 20% across the board. The breadth of companies increasing their commitments signals strong market consensus. Apple is reportedly reserving production capacity to transition its upcoming processor generations to the advanced manufacturing process. Nvidia’s increased requirements connect directly to sustained artificial intelligence chip demand. Rising AI workload needs typically translate to greater orders for TSMC’s most advanced production technologies. The trend extends beyond short-term fluctuations. TSMC’s revenue composition has been steadily tilting toward high-performance computing applications. During the second quarter of 2026, HPC accounted for 66% of TSMC’s platform-based revenue. This represents a significant increase from the 60% recorded twelve months prior. To meet escalating demand, TSMC is launching five additional 2nm fabrication plants throughout the current year. The facilities will be divided between two locations in Hsinchu and three in Kaohsiung. TSMC Senior Vice President Hou Yung-ching provided context regarding the production ramp-up scale. Initial-year 2nm wafer production is projected to exceed the company’s first-year 3nm output from 2023 by 45%. Hou further indicated that 2nm manufacturing capacity could expand at a compound annual growth rate approaching 70% between 2026 and 2028. Such aggressive growth trajectories are uncommon for semiconductor manufacturing processes. While accelerated capacity expansion appears promising, it introduces operational challenges: can TSMC activate these fabrication facilities efficiently enough to satisfy the heightened order volume? Market observers will scrutinize execution capabilities alongside demand trends. Financial analysts remain optimistic about the company’s prospects. TipRanks data shows TSM maintains a Strong Buy consensus rating, supported by six Buy recommendations and one Hold rating issued within the last three months. The consensus price target stands at $547.38, suggesting potential appreciation of approximately 21% from present trading levels. TSMC holds its position as the globe’s foremost contract semiconductor manufacturer, with its 2nm technology designed to deliver superior performance and energy efficiency compared to previous generations. These characteristics align precisely with requirements for next-generation artificial intelligence and high-performance computing applications. The current situation presents a clear picture: order volumes are expanding, manufacturing facilities are becoming operational, and the 2nm production ramp is progressing ahead of schedule.
